title: AI Use Is Rising but Spending Has Stalled, Ramp Data Shows, as Anthropic Nears IPO
excerpt: Token spend grew just 1.5% across August and September after a 42% jump in July, as price cuts and thriftier customers cap revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic.
body:
• Corporate AI token spend grew only 1.5% across August and September, down from 42% growth in July, according to Ramp transaction data reported by TechCrunch.
  • Usage volumes kept rising — the stall is in dollars, driven by API price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic and by customers routing work to cheaper models.
  • Bloomberg reported Anthropic's potential IPO valuation has slipped from about $2 trillion in early October to $1.2–1.3 trillion.
  • For Indian IT firms and startups, the signal is budget discipline: enterprise buyers are expanding AI use without expanding AI budgets.

Companies are using more artificial intelligence than ever, but they are not spending more on it. A new report from corporate card platform Ramp, reported by TechCrunch, shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose — a pattern that points to price competition and savvier customers capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic just as Anthropic prepares for its initial public offering.

According to Ramp's data, token spend grew only 1.5% across August and September. In July, it had grown 42% from the previous month. October showed a partial re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Ramp's lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

The top spenders pulled back first

Kharazian said the top 1% of firms — the heaviest AI users — stuttered in August and September, slipping just below the $10,000 per employee they had been spending at their summer peaks. Median firms spend $12 to $15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600 to $1,000, according to Ramp. A slowdown among the top cohort is, in Kharazian's words, sufficient to slow revenue entirely, even as volumes rise.

"Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies. That's fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down, they will all start to slow down simultaneously."

— Ara Kharazian, lead economist, Ramp

The mechanism is competition. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, according to TechCrunch. Anthropic answered with significant price reductions for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision the company said in a recent filing cut revenue growth by about $600 million. Meta and Nvidia are introducing cheaper enterprise offerings, open models from China and the United States are gaining ground, and customers are getting better at controlling costs: using defaults that block expensive models on long tasks, imposing employee budgets, and routing simple work to cheaper models.

What it means for the IPO

The timing matters because Anthropic is gearing up for its IPO. Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic's potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to $1.2 to $1.3 trillion, and that the company is expected to receive a high "junk" rating from credit agencies. OpenAI has also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and cut its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion, according to the Financial Times reporting cited by TechCrunch.

Kharazian's argument is not that demand is weak. Volumes are up. It is that the market has become a buyer's market, in which the same work costs less every quarter — good for customers, harder for model companies whose valuations assume breakneck revenue growth. Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data matching Ramp's pattern, summarised by TechCrunch as: tokens go up, costs come down.

What to watch

The industry's hope, Kharazian said, is a new product category — personal agents are the current candidate — that drives another wave of spending the way AI coding agents did over the past eighteen months. He is sceptical that personal agents, which he described as less economically productive than coding tools, will deliver that boost. Until such a category arrives, the Ramp data suggests enterprise AI budgets will be contested line by line — a reality Indian IT exporters and AI startups selling to US clients are already pricing into contracts.
